_comment: bb-auth access file (JSON), format version 3 — the REAL access gate (Cognito
self-signup is open). Re-checked on every /auth/validate, so an edit plus
`systemctl reload bb-auth` (SIGHUP) takes effect on the next request; a plain restart
works too. Four sibling sections, four different questions:
applications — the places, and who may reach them. This is where every grant is.
user_groups  — named sets of people, written '@name' in a scope's `groups`.
denied       — a veto. Outranks every grant, on every credential.
users        — the roster: an identity, its identifiers, and its API keys.
THE MODEL IS APPLICATION-CENTRIC. A grant is written once, on the side of the place. An
application owns a literal URL area (`base`) and a list of named scopes; a scope owns
URL patterns and one access policy; a user owns a uuid, some emails and some keys, and
NO URL at all. So 'who reaches this application?' and 'what does this application
expose?' are both one lookup instead of a scan of the whole roster.
APPLICATIONS PARTITION THE URL SPACE. Every `base` is a LITERAL prefix (no wildcards),
no two of them overlap, and every pattern of every scope must lie inside its own
application's base. A URL no application covers is REACHABLE BY NOBODY: with no
per-user URLs left, that is the only fail-closed reading, so a gated location outside
every application is a 401 for everyone. `bb-auth --check-users FILE` prints the areas.
SCOPES ARE FIRST MATCH WINS, IN FILE ORDER, inside one application. That is what makes
a carve-out expressible: put the narrow, stricter scope BEFORE the broad one, as
'healthz' and 'admin' are below. Reversed, 'everything' would answer for them and they
would never be reached. Reorder with: bb-auth-adm scope mv APP SCOPE POSITION.
ACCESS is required on every scope and has no default, because it decides everything:
anonymous     — no credential at all. The 204 names nobody.
authenticated — ANY identity Cognito vouches for, enrolled or not. Since self-signup
is open, that means anyone who can register: right for an onboarding
area, wrong for anything else. An API key never qualifies, because
Cognito vouches for no key of ours.
restricted    — the uuids in `users` and the groups in `groups`, and only through the
credential classes in `credentials` ('login' = an id_token or the
session cookie, 'api_key' = a bbk_ key; absent means both).
EXCLUDED is a scope's own veto, checked BEFORE its grant, so it beats a group the
subject is in and it beats `authenticated` — which lists nobody, so it is the only way
to keep one person out of an onboarding area. It takes a uuid, a '@group', or a bare
email for an identity the roster has never heard of, exactly as `denied` does, and an
email that does resolve is folded onto its uuid at load. It is REFUSED on `anonymous`:
that scope grants with no credential at all, so an excluded client would simply send
none. Use `denied` to shut somebody out everywhere; use this to shut them out of here.
USERS are identified by a uuid, and every reference in this file uses it. The emails
are the identifiers Cognito can vouch for, and any of them resolves to the same row, so
changing how someone signs in touches one line instead of every scope that lists them.
The tools take an email wherever they take a uuid: you never have to type one.
DENIED accepts a uuid (vetoes the user and every identifier they have) or a bare email
(vetoes an identity this file has never heard of, which on an `authenticated` scope is
the only denial that exists). It cannot revoke an id_token or a cookie mid-flight,
since those are stateless, but the very next /auth/validate denies. Note it does NOT
reach an `anonymous` scope: that scope grants with no credential at all, so a vetoed
client would simply send nothing.
KEYS are addressed by `key_hash` = SHA-256 of the bbk_ bearer (mint with
bb-auth-adm key add); the raw key is never stored here. `duration`: <n>d / <n>h / 0 /
never, counted from `released`. `scopes` is a RESTRICTION, never a grant: it limits
which of its owner's grants that key may exercise. Absent means all of them.
WILDCARDS, valid in every component of a scope pattern: `*` = any run of characters but
never `/` — EXCEPT as the final character, where it swallows the rest of the URL,
slashes included; `&` = exactly one character, never `/`. So `/app1/*` covers the whole
/app1 subtree while `/app1*` would also match /app1-admin: always put the `/` before
the `*`. And `/app1/*` does NOT match a bare `/app1`: list both.
Validate a file before deploying it: `bb-auth --check-users FILE`.
Convert an older file (one with no "version"): `bb-auth-adm migrate -f OLD -o NEW`.

applications.name: app1
applications.notes: the login page here overrides BB_AUTH_LOGIN_URL for this whole area

scopes.name: healthz
scopes.notes: listed FIRST, or 'everything' below would answer for it

scopes.name: admin
scopes.notes: a browser login only, and one member of @admins is kept out of THIS scope without being taken out of the group

scopes.name: everything
scopes.notes: the onboarding grant: anyone Cognito vouches for, enrolled or not — except the one address named here, who is in no users entry and so can be excluded no other way

scopes.name: api
scopes.notes: machines only, and only the ones enrolled here

users.notes: in @admins, so reaches app1/admin through the group
two identifiers, one identity: either one signs in as this row

api_keys.notes: example only: mint a real one with `bb-auth-adm key add bot@example.com --id laptop`
no `scopes`, so it reaches everything its owner reaches through api_key

users.notes: in @admins, and `excluded` from app1/admin: still in the group, still reaching everything else the group reaches, kept out of that one scope. NOTE neither being in no scope nor being excluded from one keeps them off an authenticated scope; that is what `denied`, or that scope's own `excluded`, is for.
